title: Office of Compliance Administrative and Technical Corrections Act of 2015
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was introduced. The expanded summary of the House passed version is repeated here.)

Office of Compliance Administrative and Technical Corrections Act of 2015

(Sec. 2) This bill amends the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 (CAA) to revise its procedures for mediation and hearings.

The Executive Director of the Office of Compliance is required to:

  • develop a master list of individuals experienced in adjudicating, arbitrating, or mediating the kinds of personnel and other matters for which mediation may be held, including, but not limited to, members of a state or District of Columbia bar and retired judges of U.S. courts; and
  • appoint individuals (mediators) from this list. Currently, mediators are appointed after the Executive Director considers recommendations by certain organizations.

Between 30 to 90 days after the end of the mediation period, a CAA-covered legislative branch employee must elect either to file a complaint with the Office or to file a civil action in the proper U.S. district court.

The Executive Director must also notify all persons participating in a mediation, hearing, or deliberation of the confidentiality requirements and of the sanctions applicable to any person who violates them.

(Sec. 3) Any individual serving as a member of the Board of Directors of the Office as of February 28, 2015, may be appointed to serve for one additional two-year term.

summary.headline: This 2015 law makes technical changes to how the Congressional Accountability Act handles mediation, complaints, and Office of Compliance board terms.
summary.what_it_does: The law changes how mediators are chosen for disputes under the Congressional Accountability Act. The Executive Director must keep a master list of experienced people, such as state bar members and retired federal judges, and pick mediators from that list instead of relying on recommendations from outside organizations. After mediation ends, a covered legislative branch employee must choose within 30 to 90 days whether to file a complaint with the Office or sue in federal district court. The law also lets a current Board of Directors member, as of February 28, 2015, serve one more two-year term.

who_it_affects.group: Congressional employees covered by the Congressional Accountability Act
who_it_affects.how: They must choose between filing a complaint with the Office of Compliance or filing a lawsuit in federal district court within 30 to 90 days after mediation ends.

who_it_affects.group: Lawyers and retired federal judges who may serve as mediators
who_it_affects.how: They can be placed on a master list and appointed to mediate workplace disputes covered by the Act.

who_it_affects.group: Members of the Office of Compliance Board of Directors
who_it_affects.how: Those serving as of February 28, 2015 may be appointed to one additional two-year term.

who_it_affects.group: People taking part in mediations, hearings, or deliberations
who_it_affects.how: They must be told about confidentiality rules and the penalties for breaking them.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted March 20, 2015; the official summary does not list separate effective dates for each change.
